primary_meaning: The eschatological ingathering of humanity at the end of the age, when God gathers the faithful and judges or separates the wicked.
primary_basis: Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43 — Jesus explicitly identifies the harvest as “the end of the age,” involving the gathering of both righteous and wicked.
Matthew 13:47–50 — the final separation of the righteous and wicked is compared to sorting a catch, closely paralleling harvest imagery.
Revelation 14:14–20 — the earth is reaped in imagery encompassing final gathering and divine judgment.
Joel 3:12–13 — a ripe harvest symbolizes the nations’ readiness for divine judgment.
Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17 — threshing and the gathering of wheat versus burning chaff depict final salvation and judgment.

alternatives.meaning: Evangelism and missionary ingathering: people who are receptive or ready to be brought into God’s kingdom, with disciples serving as laborers.
basis: Matthew 9:37–38; Luke 10:2 — the plentiful harvest and few laborers describe the need for kingdom workers.
John 4:35–38 — fields ready for harvest symbolize people ready to receive Jesus’ message.

alternatives.meaning: Divine judgment specifically, especially the destruction of wicked individuals, cities, or nations, without equal emphasis on gathering the saved.
basis: Isaiah 17:4–6 — harvesting depicts the reduction and judgment of Jacob’s glory.
Jeremiah 51:33 — Babylon is compared to a threshing floor whose harvest time is imminent.
Hosea 6:11; Joel 3:13; Revelation 14:17–20 — harvest or vintage imagery represents punitive judgment.

alternatives.meaning: Moral recompense: people eventually reap the consequences of what they sow, whether corruption or eternal life.
basis: Galatians 6:7–9 — sowing to the flesh or Spirit produces a corresponding harvest.
2 Corinthians 9:6–11 — sowing and reaping symbolize generosity and its resulting fruit.

alternatives.meaning: Resurrection, particularly the resurrection of believers following Christ as the firstfruits of a larger harvest.
basis: 1 Corinthians 15:20–23 — Christ’s resurrection is the firstfruits, implying the subsequent resurrection harvest of those who belong to him.
James 1:18 — believers are described as a kind of firstfruits of God’s creatures.

alternatives.meaning: God’s blessing, provision, abundance, and restored creation, often associated with thanksgiving or covenant faithfulness.
basis: Psalm 67:6–7 — the earth’s yield accompanies divine blessing.
Joel 2:21–27 — restored harvests signify God’s mercy and restoration.
Amos 9:13–15 — extraordinary agricultural abundance depicts eschatological restoration.

alternatives.meaning: Spiritual growth reaching maturity or ripeness before divine action.
basis: Mark 4:26–29 — the seed grows to maturity and is harvested when the grain is ripe.
Revelation 14:15 — ripeness signals that the appointed time for reaping has arrived.

notes: There is no single context-independent symbolic definition of “harvest.” The strongest and most explicit biblical identification is the end-of-the-age gathering and judgment in Matthew 13, but Christian teaching also very commonly uses harvest language for evangelism. Context determines whether the emphasis falls on salvation, judgment, missionary work, resurrection, recompense, or blessing.
